steps.title: Project
steps.text: I pick the project. Its rules, its memory and its build decisions apply to everything that follows.

steps.title: I give a task
steps.text: I send the task. The browser passes my message to Terminal.

steps.title: Terminal dispatches it
steps.text: Terminal sends the task to the agent session of the project I chose.

steps.title: Agent prepares
steps.text: A new session loads its rules; an existing one resumes with what it remembers.

steps.title: Agent works
steps.text: The agent works through the task from its rules and memory. Its tools run on my server; the model it calls runs at the provider.

steps.title: I get the result
steps.text: Terminal streams the agent’s answer back to me. What its tools built stays in the project.

entries.title: Message
entries.text: My browser sends the task to Terminal.
detail: I tell the agent what needs to change and what result I expect.

entries.title: Attachments
entries.text: Files travel with the task.
detail: Screenshots and files ride along with the message. The agent works from what I show it, not from my retelling.

entries.title: DEF / SIM
entries.text: DEF sends the ordinary task. SIM appends a short-Russian-reply instruction without restricting work or tools.
detail: DEF is the normal reply. SIM asks for a short answer in Russian while the agent still does the whole job. I read less, the work stays the same.

entries.title: Recipient & model
entries.text: The message targets the selected agent and carries the selected model.
detail: I choose the agent, the model and how hard it thinks. Each lane keeps its own picks, so switching engines and back costs me nothing.

entries.title: Save work & decisions
entries.text: Two requests I make on purpose: save the decisions, push the code.

entries.title: Engine
entries.text: The engine determines whether Claude or OpenAI carries out the task.
detail: Terminal runs the agent on the engine I chose, Claude or OpenAI, inside the project I opened.

entries.title: Smart Queuing
entries.text: How queued work waits and starts.

entries.title: Involve an agent
entries.text: An agent names a colleague in one SEND TO line. Terminal delivers the ask into that colleague’s own session; the two conversations stay separate.

entries.title: Global CLAUDE.md
entries.text: The shared rules: how agents work with me and what they are authorized to change.
detail: One rules file above every project. It says how agents verify claims, talk to me, respect ownership and finish the work they were given. Claude loads it itself; Codex is told to read it first.

entries.title: Local CLAUDE.md
entries.text: The project’s own rules file at the root of its folder. In Terminal, AGENTS.md points to the same file for the OpenAI lane.
detail: Every project folder has its own rules at the root: how to work here, the design passport, where ownership ends. The agent reads it before touching anything.

entries.title: MEMORY.md
entries.text: A project memory index with links to saved notes. It points the agent toward prior decisions; it is separate from the full conversation and MemPalace.
detail: An index of what the project already learned. Claude loads it at session start; Codex is pointed at it in its first turn.

entries.title: MemPalace
entries.text: A searchable store of saved decisions, organized by project. Agents retrieve relevant entries and save new decisions through its tools. A session-start brief can supply recent entries.
detail: MemPalace is where decisions go to survive. An agent files what we agreed, and a new session searches it before asking me again.

entries.title: Skills
entries.text: Instructions for a particular kind of work. The agent reads a relevant skill and follows its workflow. A skill can describe which tools to use.
detail: A skill is a written method for one kind of work. The agent opens the matching skill and follows it instead of improvising.

entries.title: Tools
entries.text: Tools perform actions: read or edit a file, run a command, or reach an external service. Results return to the agent so it can decide what to do next.
detail: Tools are how an agent acts: edit a file, run a command, reach a service. The result comes back and the agent decides the next step.

entries.title: Conversation history
entries.text: The session keeps a record of the conversation. Resuming a session and searching curated memory use different stores.
detail: The session keeps the whole conversation, so I can come back to it. An archive keeps every session past the CLI's own retention, and a full-text index searches all of them.

entries.title: Saved decisions
entries.text: A decision can be saved for future work in project memory or MemPalace. The agent must perform that save; a final reply alone does not guarantee it.
detail: A decision that lives only in the chat is lost. The agent writes it into memory, or the next session starts from zero.

entries.title: PREP
entries.text: Save and verify decisions.
detail: PREP is the last thing before leaving: save the decisions, then read them back to prove they landed.

entries.title: PUSH
entries.text: Commit and push changes.
detail: PUSH commits the source changes and sends them to the project's repository. The code is the record, the chat is not.

entries.title: Execution order
entries.text: One queued task after another.
detail: Queued tasks reach the agent one after another, in the order I set.

entries.title: Agent availability
entries.text: Waits until the slot can accept work.
detail: The next task waits until its agent is free. The server checks before it dispatches.

entries.title: Delayed start
entries.text: Time gates the first queued task.
detail: I set when queued work may start. The first task fires when that time comes and the agent is free.

entries.title: Server-owned queue
entries.text: Runs without an open browser.
detail: The server holds the queue. I close the browser and the work still happens.

entries.title: Ask once
entries.text: One request from an agent to a colleague.
detail: An agent names a colleague in one SEND TO line. Terminal delivers the ask into that colleague's own session, with that project's context, and brings the answer back.

entries.title: Auto Mode
entries.text: Auto Mode runs on the Terminal server.
detail: Auto Mode lets an armed pair of agents pass work back and forth through the server with my browser closed. It stops at the hop limit or when a message repeats.

entries.title: Agent onboarding
entries.text: A new session starts with an introduction to how we work and the project it belongs to.
detail: Codex is told to read the global rules, the project rules, then the memory index. Claude gets the project rules; its CLI loads the rest itself. A facts file states lane, model and mode.

entries.title: Project owners
entries.text: Agents can look up their colleagues and see who owns each project.
detail: The directory says who owns each project. Crossing into a colleague's territory means asking that colleague, never doing their work for them.

entries.title: New project
entries.text: I give the project its purpose and a place in the system.
detail: Terminal runs my project script: it prepares the workspace and the starting rules. Opening the project starts its agent's first turn.

entries.title: New agent
entries.text: The project gets its agent identity when I open it.
detail: Open a project and its agent is born, named after the folder. Its first turn reads the rules and lists the open backlog.

entries.title: Composite Keys
entries.text: I choose proven structures the project needs. Each Key carries a specification the agent builds from.
detail: Keys are proven structures I build into any project: a design passport, a health watcher. They belong to the project and outlive its agent.
Before a key is built, the agent asks its intake questions and records my answers. They stay with the key, so nobody asks twice.
Lighting a key goes ASK, intake, contract check, execution, mechanical proof, version record, LIT. Every step is journaled. Only a LIT key counts.
A weekly sweep stamps key versions, rebuilds the feed and tells me which project runs an outdated key. Silent when everything is current.

entries.title: Doors
entries.text: Rules need checks while the work is happening. Enabled gates, including Doors, catch violations and send the agent back to fix them.
detail: Doors are hooks on the Claude lane at fixed moments: task submit, before a read, after every edit, turn end. A triggered door means fix the work. Codex has none.

entries.title: Monitoring
entries.text: The project still needs watching after the agent finishes. Enrolled watchers check that it is running and delivering its declared result.
detail: Watchers check enrolled projects after launch and report a failure to Telegram, naming the owner. Health Watcher checks that the thing is up and delivers what it declared. It never repairs.

entries.title: Backlog
entries.text: Project tasks wait here until taken into work. The agent marks a delivered task for review; I confirm completion.
detail: Project tasks wait in the backlog until taken. The agent marks delivered work for review; only I close it.

entries.title: Background work
entries.text: A process can keep running after the agent’s turn ends. Terminal tracks it and can accept another message; background activity alone does not restart the agent.
detail: A process can keep running after the turn ends. Terminal tracks it and takes my next message; a background process alone never restarts the agent.

entries.title: Session start
entries.text: Return to an existing session with the context it retained. Saved project memory supplies earlier decisions when the conversation no longer holds them.
detail: I return to a session and it still holds its context. When the conversation has forgotten, saved memory remembers.

entries.title: Delivered work
entries.text: The agent reports what changed and what it checked. The resulting work stays in the project for me to use.
detail: The agent reports what changed and what it checked. The work itself stays in the project, where I use it.

entries.title: Review result
entries.text: I assess the delivered work and ask for corrections. A backlog task closes only on my confirmation.
detail: I judge the result and send it back if it is wrong. A backlog task closes on my confirmation, never on the agent's report.
LOOP is the assessment path: the agent reads the project's evidence and offers three candidates with metric, baseline, gain, cost and risk. I pick one.

entries.title: Engine switch
entries.text: Any tile runs Claude or Codex; a handover brief carries the work across.
detail: Any tile runs Claude or Codex. A switch mid-turn is refused: finish or stop first. A brief built from server state hands the work over; nothing is retyped.

entries.title: Tracks
entries.text: Which subscription pays for the tile's next turn.
detail: Three tracks per lane, one subscription each, under my alias. A tile bills its track from its next turn. A track with no key, or turned off, refuses the move.

entries.title: Live Steering
entries.text: A mid-turn message steers a Codex turn; a Claude turn receives it directly.
detail: Codex: a message mid-turn steers the running turn. Claude: the message enters the open turn directly. Terminal never parks it.

entries.title: Session end
entries.text: Kill or clear ends the session; the queue survives a clear.
detail: Kill or clear ends the session. The queue survives a clear; a kill drops it into a 14-day trash. A scheduled end leaves an epitaph line.

entries.title: Automatic memory capture
entries.text: Configured Claude hooks save to MemPalace at session stop and before compaction.
detail: On the Claude lane, hooks save memory at session stop and before compaction. Codex saves through its memory tools. PREP saves on purpose and reads it back.

entries.title: Notification to me
entries.text: Arena outcomes, Reception flags and lines forwarded to a human reach me on Telegram.
detail: Telegram carries Arena outcomes and forwarded messages to me. Reception returns a task's result to the private chat that asked. Forwarding from the browser still needs an open tab.
Reception shows execution and delivery as two facts. Execution ending makes the result available; delivery is confirmed by the courier's record only. Accepting it is my call.

entries.title: Code map
entries.text: A symbol index available through tools; configured Claude doors redirect reads and searches into it.
detail: CodeGraph indexes every symbol in the project. On the Claude lane, doors redirect whole-file reads and searches into it. Codex calls the index directly.

entries.title: Discipline feedback
entries.text: Audits of past sessions write notices the agent reads at its next start.
detail: Audits of past sessions write a notice the agent reads at its next start: its discipline score, lessons from colleagues, my rulings and my hand edits to its work.

entries.title: Turn measurements
entries.text: Every finished turn journals how long the command waited for the provider, the first streamed words and the final event; a five-minute line records server stalls.
detail: Terminal writes one line per finished turn: milliseconds to the provider, to the first word, to the end, per lane and slot. Every five minutes a line reports server stalls. No prompt text.

links: The engine a tile runs is what the switch changes.
Each lane keeps its own track; a switch flips which one bills.
Model picks are remembered per lane, tracks are assigned per lane.
The chosen model belongs to the engine that runs it.
Codex can steer a running turn; Claude receives the message directly. Queued tasks wait for availability.
A parked slot accepts a fresh message instead of steering.
One ends the retained context, the other returns to it.
The server-owned queue survives a clear.
A queued kill waits for a real idle edge, never fires into parked work.
Resume reopens the provider session record.
Onboarding reads the project's own rules.
Onboarding loads the project memory index: Claude's CLI by itself, Codex on instruction.
The session introduction lists open backlog items.
Local rules extend the shared rules.
A new project receives its starting rules.
Keys can be selected at creation.
Doors are a key; rule checks are its runtime.
Configured Claude hooks capture memory in MemPalace.
Claude hook capture complements an explicit, verified decision save.
Project memory is the other place a decision can be saved.
Backlog closure needs Wolf's confirmation after review.
PUSH persists the delivered source changes.
The recipient handle resolves through the directory.
A forwarded line can leave for a human on Telegram.
Watchers report failures to Telegram, naming the owner.
A skill names the tools to use.
Work performed by tools is what stays in the project.
Configured Claude doors redirect reads and searches into CodeGraph. Codex can call its tools directly.
Audit notices are written into the memory index the agent reads at start.

nodes.title: Wolf
detail: I set the task and decide who owns what. Agents work inside the authority I already gave them; whatever needs my call waits for it.
nodes.basis: My ownership charter and approval rules.

nodes.title: Cloudflare
detail: Cloudflare Tunnel publishes the web apps; nothing on the server listens to the internet directly. Access checks who you are before an internal app. Public sites answer anyone.
nodes.basis: The tunnel configuration and the list of Access apps.

nodes.title: Model providers
detail: Claude and Codex send the conversation to their model providers. The thinking happens there; the tools run here, or reach the hosts the project is allowed to touch.
nodes.basis: Provider dispatch in Terminal and the connected tools.

nodes.title: Connected services
detail: Agents reach the outside through tools: a GitHub repository, a headless browser for pages a plain request cannot read, a spreadsheet, an analytics feed. Each connection has its own scope.

nodes.title: Telegram
detail: Telegram carries alerts and my voice tasks. Reception takes a task from a person I granted full access and returns the result to their private chat.
nodes.basis: The notification relays and Reception's grant check.

nodes.title: The Order
detail: The Order is my server agent. It owns the shared infrastructure and the access boundaries, and it executes restarts and rebuilds itself instead of bouncing them back to me.
nodes.basis: The ownership charter, delegated exceptions included.

nodes.title: Secrets
detail: The Order keeps the shared credentials. A project operator gets the ones its grant names and none of the others.

nodes.title: Server cockpit
detail: The server cockpit shows every Docker service and carries the operations I allow over SSH. Changes to shared infrastructure go through The Order.
nodes.basis: The read-only Docker proxy and the forced-command gate.

nodes.title: Terminal
detail: Terminal is where a task lives: it opens here, runs here and comes back here. Its branches and selections stay exactly as I left them.
nodes.basis: Terminal's dispatch and the task lifecycle on this map.

nodes.title: Project agents
detail: Terminal runs one session per project. The directory says who owns what; SEND TO asks the owner instead of doing the owner's work.
nodes.basis: The project-owner directory and the collaboration relay.

nodes.title: Project services
detail: Dozens of project services run on this host behind loopback ports and the Tunnel. Some bind to the tailnet; some live on their own servers.
nodes.basis: Host container bindings and the recorded remote-host grants.

nodes.title: Memory
detail: Project notes and MemPalace carry earlier decisions into later work. They are separate from the live conversation and its session history.
nodes.basis: Project memory, the session records and the MemPalace interface.

nodes.title: Tools & workspace
detail: Tools read and change project work within what the project was authorized to do. What a tool can do and what it may do are two different questions.

nodes.title: Project operators
detail: Project operators deploy, restart and read logs within my recorded grants, remote hosts included. Shared infrastructure stays with The Order. Scheduled work runs on host cron or inside services.

nodes.title: Run records
detail: Session history and mechanism journals keep what happened. An agent's final answer is a claim; the journal is the proof.
nodes.basis: The logging rule: every mechanism leaves a trail.

nodes.title: Watchers
detail: Watchers probe enrolled projects and report failures. Trivy scans images and hosts for vulnerabilities. They report; repairing is a person's job.
nodes.basis: The watcher runner and its heartbeat.

nodes.title: Recovery
detail: Restic copies selected state off the server every night, encrypted. Coverage has exclusions. A snapshot counts once it exists and a restore has been tested.
nodes.basis: Backup configuration and the backup log.

nodes.title: Other hosts
detail: Some projects run on machines outside this server. Each has a wrapper its agent uses to deploy, restart and read logs there. Production stays behind a gate.

nodes.title: Backup storage
detail: Restic copies selected state off-site; the GitHub mirror copies eligible repositories. Both have exclusions. Recovery is proven by a successful copy and a tested restore.
nodes.basis: The mirror configuration and its run log; the Restic snapshot list.
